narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 79% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest factors pushing the model toward predicting failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly suggested difficulty passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.10 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so it provided a modest positive signal that partially offset the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 27, family income in the middle bracket, and plan to attend full-time also played smaller roles, but none were strong enough to overcome the effect of your low class standing.

You should focus on improving your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Strengthening these areas will improve both your bar exam prospects and your chances in future applications.
